items.title: The things you can now do directly in the browser
items.content:
🚀 Frontend Focus

#​768 — November 25, 2026 | Read on the web

Things You Can Do With a Browser in 2027 — Luigi returns with a sequel to the popular browser-2020 list, highlighting some of the lesser-known things browsers can do today, including HTML-in-Canvas, the <model> element, HDR, on-device AI, hardware APIs, and more. Each feature is quickly explained alongside a browser support table.

Luigi De Rosa

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous verifies every UI change, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

Nudeps: npm Imports in the Browser — A new tool from Lea Verou and Dmitry Sharabin that lets you npm install packages and import them by name directly within the browser, no bundler required. It builds upon thinking outlined in Lea's 'Web dependencies are broken' article from earlier this year.

Lea Verou

When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next? — A post that takes stock of the year we've had, where the AI bubble has undoubtedly reshaped the industry. Andy argues that developers are more than "code slingers," and makes the case for investing in people, building by hand, and keeping independent publishing alive.

Andy Bell

⚡️ IN BRIEF

  • 🦊 Firefox 161 is out and adds support for the CSS random() function (more on that later), plus Compression Dictionary Transport.

  • 🐞 The Ladybird browser (an effort to build a new browser engine from scratch) is now in alpha, available for macOS and Linux. You can download it here.

  • ⚙️ Simon Willison has been trying the above Ladybird alpha and shares his initial thoughts here, calling it an "astonishingly ambitious project".

📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials

Why There Are Still No Non-WebKit Browsers on iOS — Mozilla says that, three years on, the EU's DMA (along with Japan's newer rules) has ultimately failed to open up iOS to any non-WebKit browser engines.

Mozilla

💡 After an open letter from Mozilla, Shopify and others, the European Commission says it's in talks with Apple, and Chrome's team has backed Mozilla's stance too.

Understanding CSS random() — As mentioned above, Firefox 161 has joined Chrome and Safari in supporting random(). Here, Mat uses it to give his sidenotes a hand-placed 'jauntiness'.

Mat Marquis

Foxit Compares 10 HTML to PDF APIs — Rendering engines, CSS and JavaScript handling, headers and footers, and how each API bills a render.

Foxit sponsor

Has the Web Stopped Getting Heavier? — The pace at which web pages get heavier is levelling off, as HTTP Archive data shows growth has slowed to a crawl, with the median mobile page adding just 7KB of JavaScript in the past year.

Sander van Surksum

Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality — CSS Grid really changed what was possible for page layouts, but Andy notes that designers still lean heavily on the twelve-column pattern. So he explores some more ambitious layout options that can be easily achieved today.

Andy Clarke

Playing with CSS Layers — A fun tinkering post from Kitty, experimenting with CSS layers on their personal site just for the joy of it.

Kitty Giraudel

The Compacting Sidebar Blues — What should an app's sidebar do on a screen that's too short for it? Chris explains why a scroll-state() query loops infinitely here, and what works better instead.

Chris Coyier

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?
Andrew Chung

A New Set of HTML Insertion and Streaming APIs
Amit Merchant

Creating Diagrams and Graphs Using Modern CSS
Temani Afif

🧰 Tools, Code & Resources

Button Sounds: Tactile SFX for Your UI — Josh has pulled together a free collection of 50+ professionally recorded multi-sampled clicks and toggles. Many have the charming thunks and clunks of your favorite keyboard. Distributed as an NPM package with optional React bindings.

Josh W. Comeau

Your Chart Isn’t Slow. Its Query Is — TimescaleDB extends Postgres so dashboards stay fast as data grows. $1000 credit on Tiger Cloud.

Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) sponsor

Alloy CSS: One Stylesheet for the HTML Your Server Renders — A free kit of dialogs, menus, drawers, tabs and toast notifications that all work with JavaScript turned off.

Fandy Pradana

🤖 wllama 4.0: Run llama.cpp Models in the Browser — These WebAssembly bindings for llama.cpp let you run GGUF models directly in-browser. v4 doubles inference speed, and models of any size now load, with WebGPU helping out (where available). Try the demos here.

Xuan-Son Nguyen

⏱️ <relative-time> 5.5: Format Timestamps as a Localized Relative Time — Supply this web component with a standard date/time and it'll render "2 days ago", say. GitHub uses this on its repo and code views.

GitHub

'CodePen Commander' Brings Pens into Your Local Editor — If you use CodePen Pro, Bramus has built a CLI tool that brings git-style clone/push workflows to CodePen 2.0, along with batch syncing, a local dev server, and one-command deploys.

Bramus Van Damme

Intro.js: A User-Friendly 'Onboarding Tour' Library — A library for creating step-by-step product tours (as seen during onboarding in SaaS tools, for example). It's AGPL licensed with an optional paid license available too.

Afshin Mehrabani

Port Menu: A Tiny macOS Menu Bar App To Track Dev Servers Across Projects
Eduard Wieandt

📰 Classifieds

⚡ AI agents ignore rules. Nexity’s reviewer agents check every new Next.js + Sanity section against yours: design, schema, GROQ.

🕹️ ...and finally

Kirupa’s 404 Arcade — Kirupa turned his 404 page into an awesome arcade with sixteen playable games (riffing on many a classic), complete with synthesized sound, retro stylings, and high-score tables. I mean, why not have some fun if you get lost? Very cool!

Kirupa

🖊️ If you prefer something a bit more practical, yet still with some whimsy, Ductus is a neat site that converts your handwriting into a font (OpenType or WOFF2). You can draw the letters right on the page for it to convert.

items.title: What developers think of HTML right now
items.content:
🚀 Frontend Focus

#​767 — November 18, 2026 | Read on the web

🗳️ The State of HTML 2026 Results

The State of HTML 2026 results are now out covering what developers are using, loving and struggling with, plus how much they use AI. Declarative, element-based features are winners, while form controls remain difficult. Some highlights:

  • <details>/<summary> (72.5%) and <dialog> (67.8%) are the most used interactivity features, and use of the Popover API has reached 40% now that it works in every major browser.

  • <select> and date inputs are the hardest elements to style, and customizable select is the feature most held back by browser support (Firefox is yet to ship it).

  • <datalist> usage jumped from 30% to 44%, yet positive sentiment fell from 44% to 34%, with respondents citing styling, accessibility and browser bugs.

  • Native data tables with built-in sorting and filtering topped the wishlist, ahead of tabs, comboboxes and switches. HTML includes came up again.

In his overall conclusion, Polypane creator Kilian Valkhof sees the frustration shifting from browsers doing things differently to browsers simply not having caught up yet, with mobile OSes a particular sore spot. He ends: "Our industry might be in turmoil, but I think our foundation is in good shape."

Devographics

A Form Platform That Fits Your App — Design complex forms visually and render them in React, Angular, or Vue. Keep full control over your backend and data. Create custom themes or use style adapters, extract form responses from PDFs and images with AI, and generate or fill existing PDF forms.

SurveyJS sponsor

🤖 Top 10 Things AI Gets Wrong in Web Development — The Chrome team tested frontier coding agents and found they pass only about 50% of web best-practice checks unguided, but ~90% with Modern Web Guidance installed. The areas they get wrong include accessibility, performance and security.

Philip Walton (Google)

Introducing the Cross-Origin Storage API — A new API proposal from the Chrome team to enable sites to share large assets (like AI models, fonts, common libraries, etc.) meaning end users would save bandwidth by only having to download them once.

Thomas Steiner

⚡️ IN BRIEF

  • 🔦 jQuery 4.1 and 3.8 are out. 3.8 is the last planned feature release of the 3.x line, which now gets critical fixes only.

  • 📑 Or perhaps you don't need jQuery at all? The long-standing 'You Don't Need jQuery' guide has had a major update, swapping IE fallbacks for modern one-liners.

  • 🌐 Chrome 158 is now stable, with the install element, media state pseudo-classes like :playing and :paused, and the start of XSLT's staged removal. Plus there's a look at what's new in the DevTools.

  • ⛓️‍💥 A cautionary tale about using link shorteners: some old Bitly links were recently hijacked, repurposing where they sent people.

  • 🌅 As we mentioned last month, Arc is going away on December 22, so Chris Coyier rounds up the browsers worth trying instead.

📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials

Charts in HTML and CSS — A neat gallery of column and bar charts, heatmaps, donuts, line charts and more, built from just HTML and CSS (no JavaScript or SVGs). It's all built upon semantic markup, so if you strip away the stylesheet, they remain readable tables or lists. There's also an agent skill.

Keith Cirkel

Charts That Do Analytics? Yes, With One Script — Give your users forecasts and anomaly detection in the chart itself. Orbit for Highcharts, free for 60 days.

Highcharts sponsor

The CSS caret-* Properties and Custom Caret Accessibility — A thorough look at the newer caret-shape and caret-animation properties alongside caret-color for styling the text cursor. Covers caret browsing, WCAG rules, and how author styles can trump users' caret preferences.

Sara Soueidan

What Safari on Apple HomeView Means for Your Site — Safari now runs on Apple's square, 7-inch, voice-driven display. Most sites 'just work' but Jen flags some assumptions that break, like a shorter viewport than usual, an iOS user agent on a non-iPhone, and voice users who need labeled controls.

Jen Simmons (WebKit)

PropFLIP: Because It Flips with Props — Adam takes four @property custom properties and uses them, along with a transition, to create a neat flip effect. A sprinkling of JS helps bring it all together.

Adam Argyle

Giving AI Agents a Better Way to Debug CSS
Amit Merchant

Building an atproto Link Aggregator
Johanna Larsson

🧰 Tools, Code & Resources

Allo: Your Friendly Neighborhood Font — A really nice, free, open source typeface with variable weights and roundness options, automatic optical sizing, plenty of alternates, and much more. The site does an excellent job of showing it all off. Repo here.

Josh Puckett

📊 Who Shipped First? Chromium vs Gecko vs WebKit — A look at 'which browser engine got there first' for a huge range of Web platform features. Patrick used the web-features data for this and Chromium/Chrome, perhaps unsurprisingly, has a clear lead in introducing new features.

Patrick Brosset

Your Chart Renders Fast. The Query Behind It Doesn’t — Tiger Cloud keeps dashboard queries fast as data grows, and it’s still Postgres underneath. $1000 credit to start.

Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) sponsor

🐞 BugShot: Chromium Extension for Streamlined Bug Reporting — Adds a side panel for turning browser bugs into a report that includes captures, annotations, recordings, and logs. It can then submit reports directly to Jira, GitHub, Linear, Notion, and more.

SinhyeokKang

Astrobook: A Minimal Storybook Alternative — An alternative to the popular Storybook UI component playground that supports React, Vue, Preact, Svelte, Solid, Lit, and Astro. The demo site includes multiple framework examples.

Ocavue

Aura: Ambient Gradients Built from Layered CSS Blend Modes — 200+ customizable gradients that offer a soft, atmospheric look that feels 'like light'. Click any gradient to preview it live, browse sub-categories (mesh, nebula, lattice, glass, etc.), and export as PNG, SVG, CSS, Tailwind, etc. GitHub repo.

Cristian Olivera

📰 Classifieds

⚡️ Add lightning-fast 1D/2D barcode scanning to your web app with STRICH. On-device processing, free trial and demo!

📱 No Mac needed. Expo Simulators gives your coding agent a cloud iOS Simulator to test its own work, on Linux or Windows.

🧾 Generating invoices or reports from JSON? Foxit compares 10 PDF generator APIs on templates, HTML rendering and how each one bills.

🥽 ...and finally

WebKit Previews Spatial CSS — An early look at arranging 3D <model> objects on the web with plain CSS with which you can group them in a shared space, snap them together, and tweak the lighting. A JavaScript call can even pop the scene out into the room around you. Safari on visionOS only, behind a flag (remember Vision Pro?).

Brandel Zachernuk (WebKit)

items.title: Responsive design is more than resizing a window
items.content:
🚀 Frontend Focus

#​766 — November 11, 2026 | Read on the web

Beyond the Viewport: Introducing Site Seeing — Making a design responsive means tackling more than just resizing, with real users often having on-screen keyboards, split views, docked DevTools, and other things open, or even using oddly sized in-app browsers. Ahmad's new, free browser-based tool is designed to preview your layouts in these awkward contexts.

Ahmad Shadeed

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

🤖 Modern Web Guidance 1.0: Web Expertise for AI Agents — Coding agents can write good code, but tend to fall behind on Web standards and best practices. Chrome's skills for steering agents toward modern, Baseline-aware HTML/CSS are now stable, and it's not just Google: Lea Verou, Patrick Brosset (Edge), and Jake Archibald (Firefox) are among the project's owners.

Philip Walton (Google)

The Web is More Than Enough — An encouraging reminder of the immense power of the Web platform and how advanced use of WebAssembly, Web Crypto, WebGL, and Web Audio is increasingly within the reach of developers to build apps you'd once never have imagined in the browser.

Paul Ford

⚡️ IN BRIEF

  • 🗳️ The State of JS survey for 2026 is open now and seeking responses.

  • 🦊 Firefox 160 is now stable. On-device speech recognition via the Web Speech API arrives on desktop, and you can experiment with blocking="render" and lazy loading for video and audio behind flags.

  • ♿ GitHub now recognizes an ACCESSIBILITY.md file and surfaces it on a repository's overview page.

  • 🦓 Zigzag is a new lightweight browser for macOS, coming in at just 18MB.

📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials

Computing with CSS Layout — How much can CSS 'compute' on its own? Leaning on the behavior of CSS grid, flexbox, and more, this interactive piece shows how to read CSS's 'calculations' back as numbers and put them to practical use, including drawing animated charts.

Agustin Capeletto

System Colors Need to Work Together — You might expect paired CSS system colors like HighlightText and Highlight to be readable together, but in Chrome on Android's dark mode they manage a contrast ratio of only 1.98:1. Aaron's cross-browser study shows which pairs hold up.

Aaron Gustafson

How to Build Your Own Automated Debugging Workflow — Connect your coding agent to Sentry and turn errors into fix PRs. See the guides and recipes in the resource hub.

Sentry sponsor

Is 'Using Declarations Just Once' Still Effective in CSS? — This classic optimization technique merges repeated declarations under one grouped selector. Jens built a tool to test it on 30 real sites and found it can still cut uncompressed file size, if applied selectively.

Jens Oliver Meiert

Local Visual Regression Testing for Agents with Playwright — A look at using Playwright's toHaveScreenshot matcher to give coding agents a consistent local visual-feedback loop.

Paolo Ricciuti

Building Interfaces That Understand What Users Want to Do — A look at using small AI 'decision models' to pick from options you define, including via Chrome's experimental, on-device Decisions API.

Agustin Barrientos

CSS-Tricks, Version 20 — Now under new ownership, the site is getting JavaScript cleanup, a Sass reorganization, and more, which Geoff explains in detail.

Geoff Graham

A Groundbreaking Upgrade to SVG is Approaching: Linked Parameters are Almost Here
Roman Komarov

Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
Eric Bailey

Re-Implementing :nth-child() with Modern CSS
Temani Afif

🧰 Tools, Code & Resources

Marcos Iglesias

The “Export CSV” Button Shouldn’t Time Out — Exports scan every row in the range and slow as data grows. TimescaleDB keeps them fast. $1000 credit on Tiger Cloud.

Clearleft

items.title: Safari will 'dark mode' your site for you
items.content:
🚀 Frontend Focus

#​765 — November 4, 2026 | Read on the web

Safari Introduces Adaptive Dark Mode — A new (opt-in) feature added to the Safari 27.3 beta that automatically adapts light sites to dark ones. It's here because although around 40% of pages are loaded by users using dark mode, only 10% of page loads directly support it.

WebKit

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous verifies every UI change, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex — Swapping JavaScript for container queries and :has() can cut your code down but introduce bugs elsewhere in your layout. Gabriel shares four examples, including why container-type can collapse flex items to zero width.

Gabriel Shoyombo

📊 Design Systems Should Be Fast by Default — Den benchmarks dropdowns and checkbox lists across ten popular design systems, diagnoses the slowdowns, and shares tests to catch regressions.

Den Odell

⚡️ IN BRIEF

  • 🤚 The CSSWG has resolved that form controls get cursor: pointer by default under appearance: base. Cory LaViska explains the data and the objections.

  • 🌐 Chrome 158 is in beta (stable due November 17) with the <install> element, media pseudo-classes like :playing and :paused, ::highlight(*), and XSLT is on its way out.

  • 🆕 Rachel Andrew shares an update on changes to the web platform in October, including scroll-driven animations gaining support across all major engines.

  • 🧰 Chrome DevTools has added a visual position-area editor in Elements, Web Install manifest diagnostics, and MCP server improvements.

  • 🤖 Google will support a shared AI training control in robots.txt, based on IETF AIPREF work, letting sites set a preference once for multiple AI providers.

📙 Articles, Opinions & Tutorials

Native Masonry Layouts with CSS Grid Lanes — A practical guide to native masonry layouts with CSS Grid Lanes, covering placement, fit-tolerance, horizontal layouts, subgrid and source-order accessibility. It's supported in only Safari right now, but other engines are working on it.

Saleh Mubashar

Making Features Generic in CSS — Rachel takes a look at the new flow-start and flow-end alignment keywords, and touches upon why the CSSWG often renames things.

Rachel Andrew

Embeddable Forms With Bookings, Live Pricing, and Payments Built In — Build it visually, paste two lines into any site. Unlimited submissions on every plan with spam protection. From €6/mo.

CraftForms sponsor

Quirks and Vintage Uses of CSS Table Display — Looks back at display: table and its related values, sharing what each does and the pre-flexbox tricks they enabled — while of course noting that you probably shouldn't reach for them today. A neat history lesson.

Declan Chidlow

🧡 If You Love a Website, Back It Up — Following one of their favorite websites disappearing, a web-archiving practitioner explains how to go about preserving sites for yourself. A practical tour of browser-based capture techniques, automated crawling, and embedding the results.

Misty De Meo

Spreading Liquid with Three.js — A technical walkthrough of a neat liquid-spreading effect (built for a cosmetics campaign). It shows off using a height map for thickness, a velocity map for movement, and fragment shaders to render the result. There's a satisfying demo to play with, too.

MISAKI NAKANO

How a Split Webfont Slowed Down Text Layout — A font splitter put i and j in a different file from the rest of the alphabet, forcing extra text-shaping work within words (causing INP to suffer). Here's why, plus a script to check your own font CSS.

Ivan Kristianto

Why Is the Analytics Tab the Slowest Page in Your App? — Usually it's one query scanning months of rows. TimescaleDB extends Postgres to make it fast. Get $1000 credit.

Tiger Data (creators of TimescaleDB) sponsor

Multi-Column Different-Speed Scrolling — There are some fun scrolling experiments here thanks to scroll-driven animations.

Chris Coyier

Useful @custom-media Presets
Daniel Schwarz

⚠️ Third-Party Scripts

Last week we shared a PSA about forgotten script tags and how what they load can be hijacked. Days later, a similar attack prominently appeared in the wild.

On October 29, a performance monitoring script on Polymarket was swapped for a wallet drainer. The URL of the script didn't change, just the payload, so the CSP let it through, but Scott Helme's write-up explains what would have stopped it.

Whatever you load from third parties, it's worth auditing for security, privacy, and performance reasons. Some steps worth taking:

  • Pin scripts with Subresource Integrity where the vendor's file is static, and use the new Integrity-Policy-Report-Only header to find any you've missed.
  • Self-host third-party resources where you can. Request Metrics explains how it protects its own agent and why it's safe to self-host.
  • Load third-party JavaScript efficiently, or use Partytown to move it off the main thread entirely.
  • Audit what your page is loading with Request Map and Third Party Web.

Lastly, if you provide third-party scripts to users, check out Jack Ellis's writeup of how Fathom Analytics keeps their analytics script secure for some tips.

🧰 Tools, Code & Resources

sidebearing-trim: Align Text by 'Visible Ink', Not by Glyph Boxes — You can try it out interactively on the page and there's a write-up of why you should care here. One of those things that designers, in particular, are likely to notice! 😅 GitHub repo.

Pekka Lammi

🎨 ColorSym: Symbols to Identify Colors 'When Color Alone Isn't Enough' — A way to use symbols to supplement colors, aiding with accessibility. The symbols are 'intelligent' where, for example, the orange symbol is a combo of those for red and yellow. Available as SVGs or a custom font.

Chris Eastridge & Luis Francisco

Astrotypes: Curated Font Pairings for Astro — Search and preview font pairings sourced from Google Fonts, Bunny CDN, and Fontshare live on the page. Each pair has a copy command for various tools (npm, Yarn, Bun, etc).

Michael Andreuzza

File Viewer: A Browser-Native Office, PDF, CAD, and Archive Viewer for Internal Web Apps — Provides read-only views for Office, PDF/OFD, CAD, archives, email and more, with integrations for React, Vue, and Svelte. There's also a live demo to try.

Flyfish Dev

📰 Classifieds

Know React? Then you and your coding agent can ship iOS and Android apps. Expo runs the builds and CI/CD and gets you into the app stores.

🧪 In-browser testing inside your dev server. TWD adds a test sidebar next to your app, and your AI agent runs it too. Free and MIT.

🔤 ...and finally

Introducing Geist Serif — Vercel's Geist family gains a high-contrast display serif for headlines, built on the same metrics as Geist Sans so the two mix cleanly. Geist Sans, Geist Mono and Geist Pixel are on Google Fonts already; Serif isn't yet, but will be in due course.

Vercel
